title: Using Reinforcement Learning to Train Large Language Models to Explain Human Decisions
claim: A shared backbone is post-trained by three strategies; ours uses RL on sampled reasoning completions instead of direct supervised targets.
layout: Single panel, left-to-right fork into three rows, example completions boxed on right
description: A left-to-right diagram. On the left, the text 'backbone LLM' sits above a Qwen2.5 logo, with an arrow to 'LoRA modules'. From there, a branching arrow splits into three rows labeled SFT, Centaur-style SFT and RL. A black-tabbed box at the top right shows the prompt q, 'Problem 10621 in the training set'. It describes a choice between a sure $27 and a gamble. Each row has rounded boxes with example model outputs in JSON. SFT shows one box with the whole JSON block highlighted in light blue. Centaur-style SFT shows one box with only the numbers inside << >> highlighted. RL shows three boxes, o1, o2 and o3, each with a short chain-of-thought and a different JSON prediction, with the numbers highlighted. Light-blue highlights show which tokens each method trains on or rewards.
caption: Overview of three post-training strategies for building cognitive models of human risky choice using Qwen-2.5-7B-Instruct. The backbone LLM was first adapted using low-rank adaptation (LoRA) [ref], followed by post-training via three strategies: supervised fine-tuning (SFT), Centaur-style SFT [ref], and reinforcement learning from outcome-based rewards [ref]. In the illustrated example, the LLM is prompted to predict human choice behavior. SFT and Centaur-style models are trained directly on human data represented in JSON format. In contrast, the RL model generates candidate completions that include CoT reasoning and final predictions in JSON format, with each completion evaluated based on its predictions. Tokens or predictions relevant to each training method are highlighted in light blue.
abstract: A central goal of cognitive modeling is to develop models that not only predict human behavior but also provide insight into the underlying cognitive mechanisms. While neural network models trained on large-scale behavioral data often achieve strong predictive performance, they typically fall short in offering interpretable explanations of the cognitive processes they capture. In this work, we explore the potential of pretrained large language models (LLMs) to serve as dual-purpose cognitive models--capable of both accurate prediction and interpretable explanation in natural language. Specifically, we employ reinforcement learning with outcome-based rewards to guide LLMs toward generating explicit reasoning traces for explaining human risky choices. Our findings demonstrate that this approach produces high-quality explanations alongside strong quantitative predictions of human decisions.
